doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 5, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Closing words from the book and loving the stage
summary: Rowe reads the book's final line; Gibbs says he is most comfortable on stage, banters with audiences, and tells how Frank Rossolino yodeled with the Dream Band.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: Well I’ve really enjoyed this and I want to close with the last thing you wrote in your book, and it said, “Even though we know that into each life a little rain must fall, all in all I’ve been very fortunate for I’ve been able to laugh all the way to the bandstand.”

Yeah well it’s true. It really is true, Monk. I’ve been fortunate. ‘Cause I looked forward to getting on stage. I’m at my most comfortable when I’m on stage. Because I don’t work, I have fun. I mean I include my audience, that’s why I don’t like playing big concerts. If I play for people playing in a ballroom at least the audience is close, they’re about two feet away from me so I can tell the guy to get a toupee or whatever, I’m going to tell the guy. Lady get your nose fixed, or whatever it is. I become Don Rickles all of a sudden. But you know what we become friends and they think they’re at a party. And it’s sort of like my band is always partying anyhow. When we get together it’s a party. Because I like to laugh and like I said, I’ll play straight for Jack Sheldon, Frank Rossolino, Conte Candoli, Med Flory, these are funny minds. If they want to say something I’ll say, “What is it?” and I’ll feed them lines. And you know what’s wild? A lot of times, Frank Rossolino, I’ve got to tell you, with the Dream Band. Frank — everybody loved Frank Rossolino and the band. He was one of the funniest people. And I have a habit of going [claps] here it is, and I always give them the tempo. And you do this for about two, three minutes, and the audience they’d be yelling “here it is” and everybody yelled. And I’d say, “One, two,” and I’d say, “hey Frank.” And I’d ask him any question. “How’s your mother,” “how’s your foot,” “how’s your car.” And he’d get up, Frank would jump up and stomp, and he would start saying the most ridiculous thing, and Frank could yodel by the way, he really could yodel. And he’d wind up yodeling, which had nothing to do with anything. The audience was in stitches. We already won the — we could have played “The Star Spangled Banner” and they would have stood up and cheered. You know.
